passage: "Keerthana, hop to it!" Joseph Sir shouted across the ground. So Keerthana hopped, both feet together, all the way to the line. A few children laughed. Her cheeks burned. She had done exactly what he said. The drill went on, whistles and forty voices bouncing off the school wall, until her head felt packed with cotton. Joseph Sir didn't send her to stand in the corner. At the water tap he crouched to her level. "My mistake. 'Hop to it' is a saying. It only means come quickly. You weren't wrong to hop." Keerthana nodded slowly. "Can you just say come quickly next time?" "Deal. And if the whistles get too much, you can stand by the tap for a minute."

qa.q: What does Joseph Sir say 'hop to it' means?
qa.a: It only means come quickly.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when the children laughed, and why?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and confused, with burning cheeks, because she had done exactly what he said.

qa.q: Which choice by Joseph Sir turned the moment around?
qa.a: Instead of punishing her, he explained the saying clearly and kindly, owned his mistake and offered a quiet spot by the tap.

qa.q: If Joseph Sir had sent Keerthana to the corner, what would change?
qa.a: She would learn that taking words literally gets her punished, and she would feel more ashamed and more tired, not less confused.

grounding: It shows a child who takes words literally and is worn out by school noise, helped by a clear, kind explanation instead of punishment.

passage: My name's Dhruv and I sit next to Charu, so I saw most of it. At break she walked straight into the middle of the skipping rope while Mitali's group was counting. The rope smacked her leg and they all shouted, "You can't just barge in!" Charu stood very still. Then she asked, "Where is that written?" They thought she was being cheeky. I don't think she was. She looked like she really wanted to know. Last period she had her head on her desk and her fingers in her ears, though only the fan was going. Ma'am saw and didn't scold. Next morning a card was pinned by the door: Skipping - wait at the end and ask, "Can I jump in?" Charu read it twice. At break she waited at the end of the line.

qa.q: What rule was written on the card by the door?
qa.a: Wait at the end and ask, 'Can I jump in?'

qa.q: How does Dhruv think Charu felt when she asked, 'Where is that written?'
qa.a: Dhruv thinks she was genuinely confused and curious, not cheeky, because she looked like she really wanted to know.

qa.q: What made the difference for Charu the next day?
qa.a: Ma'am wrote the unspoken rule down clearly instead of scolding, so Charu could read it and follow it.

qa.q: How might Mitali's group see Charu differently if someone explained what happened?
qa.a: They might see that Charu didn't know the unwritten rule, rather than thinking she was being rude or cheeky.

passage: Class note, Year 3, Wednesday. Before assembly I told the children, "Pull your socks up." Uday bent down and pulled up his socks, then looked puzzled when others giggled. At break, Preeti shouted, "You're it!" and ran. Uday stood still and then asked me, "It what?" He had been told off for "ignoring the game" last week. After lunch he put his head down on the desk and covered his ears; the hall had been very noisy. Next: I drew the tag rules as three simple pictures on a card for him and explained "pull your socks up" can also mean "try harder". He kept the card in his pocket.

qa.a: He seemed tired and overwhelmed after the very noisy hall, and needed a break from the sound.

qa.q: Which response helped Uday more than a telling-off?
qa.a: The picture card with the tag rules and a clear explanation of the phrase helped, instead of scolding him for ignoring the game.

qa.q: How might Preeti see the moment when Uday stood still?
qa.a: Preeti might think Uday did not want to play, when really he did not understand what "You're it" meant.

passage:
Dear diary,
Today in PE Simran Ma'am said, "Hop to it!" so I hopped. Everyone laughed. I did not know why.
At lunch the girls played a game with a rope and said I was out. I don't know how I was out. I asked twice and Riddhi rolled her eyes.
The bell is SO loud. By the last period my head felt like it was full of bees.
After school Simran Ma'am called me and said, "Bhavna, 'hop to it' means hurry. I should have been clearer." She wrote it in my notebook. Now I have a page called Funny Sayings.
At home I lay under the dining table for a long time. Mumma let me.

qa.q: What does "hop to it" mean, according to Simran Ma'am?
qa.a: She said "hop to it" means hurry.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel by the last period, and why?
qa.a: Bhavna felt exhausted and overwhelmed, saying it was like having a head full of bees after the loud bell and a confusing day.

qa.q: What did Simran Ma'am do well after PE?
qa.a: She took responsibility for being unclear, explained the phrase kindly and wrote it in Bhavna's notebook instead of scolding.

qa.q: What is it like for Mumma when Bhavna lies under the dining table?
qa.a: Mumma may understand that Bhavna needs quiet rest after a hard day, and chooses to let it happen rather than push for talk.

grounding: Shows a child who takes words literally, is confused by playground rules and exhausted by school noise, helped by a kind, clear explanation.

passage:
In the school playground in Uppsala, Leila stood still while the others ran. "You're it!" Oskar shouted, tagging her as he ran past. Leila frowned. She had not agreed to be anything.
Later in class, Ms Ulla said, "Leila, pull your socks up, your spelling is slipping." Leila bent down and pulled up her socks. Two boys laughed. Leila's face went hot; she didn't know what she had done wrong.
By three o'clock, the scraping chairs and shouting felt like sandpaper in her head. She put her head on the desk.
Ms Ulla crouched beside her. "I'm sorry, that was a saying. I meant please try harder with spelling. Next time I'll say exactly what I mean." She drew the tag rules as three pictures on a card. Leila studied them, and her shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: What did Leila do when Ms Ulla told her to pull her socks up?
qa.a: She bent down and pulled up her socks.

qa.q: How did Leila feel when the two boys laughed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and confused, her face hot, because she didn't know what she had done wrong.

qa.q: Which of Ms Ulla's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Apologising, saying exactly what she meant and drawing the rules as pictures helped far more than any telling-off, because Leila could understand clearly.

qa.q: How might Oskar see Leila standing still after he tagged her?
qa.a: He might think she was being unfriendly or odd, without knowing the game's rules just weren't clear to her.

grounding: Leila takes words literally, finds playground rules confusing and is exhausted by school noise, and clear, kind explanations help her.
